## Task
**Tree-node operations in xarray**

In this xarray repository, the basic tree structure that DataTree is built on (the TreeNode class,
plus group_subtrees and zip_subtrees) does not work: parts of the code it relies on are missing.
Make it work, so that a user can:

- look up an object in a tree by a Unix-like path: a path starting with "/" is resolved from the
  topmost node of the tree (whose own name is not a path part), any other path from the current
  node; ".." moves up one node, "." and "" stay put. A path that leads nowhere, or ".." from the
  top node, raises a KeyError;
- put an item into a tree at such a path: optionally creating missing intermediate nodes (of the
  same type as the current node) and optionally refusing to overwrite an existing node. A path
  with no final name ("." or "/") raises a ValueError (a trailing slash after a name keeps that
  name); an unreachable target without node creation raises a KeyError whose message contains
  "Could not reach"; an existing node with overwriting refused raises a KeyError whose message
  contains "Already a node object";
- move a node under a new parent under a given child name, or detach it: a new parent that is
  not a tree node raises a TypeError; making a node its own parent, or the child of one of its own
  descendants, raises the tree's invalid-tree error (messages containing "cannot be a parent of
  itself" and "is already a descendant") before anything changes; asking for a different parent
  without a child name raises a ValueError; asking for the parent it already has changes nothing,
  whatever name is given. Detaching a node removes it from its parent's children and leaves it
  as the top of its own intact tree (doing so on a top node has no effect);
- ask a node about its place in the tree:
  - the tuple of nodes above it, closest first (empty at the top);
  - the topmost node of its tree (itself at the top);
  - the nodes that share its parent, as a new dict by name in the parent's order, without itself
    (empty at the top);
  - its level (0 at the top, +1 per step down); the tree's depth (the greatest level anywhere in
    the same tree, the same from every node; 0 for a single node); and the width (how many nodes
    in the whole tree share its level, across all branches);
  - all nodes below it, breadth-first, excluding itself; the nodes below it that have no
    children, breadth-first (itself if it has none);
  - an iteration over itself and everything below it, breadth-first; and the same with each
    node's relative POSIX path ("." for itself, then "child1", "child2", "child1/grandchild");
  - two deprecated views that emit a deprecation warning on every access: the chain from the top
    node down to and including itself, and the chain from itself up to and including the top node;
- iterate over several trees at once with group_subtrees (yielding each relative path with the
  tuple of matching nodes) or zip_subtrees (yielding only the node tuples), breadth-first, with
  paths and order following the first tree (child order may differ between trees). Calling either
  with no trees raises a TypeError. If the trees' child names differ at some node, the error
  for non-matching tree structure is raised only when iteration reaches it; at the top it reads
  "children at root node do not match: <names> vs <names>".

Find out where in the codebase these pieces belong and implement them so that they fit the rest
of xarray. All dependencies are installed; do not install anything.

# xarray development setup

## Setup

```bash
uv sync
```

## Run tests

```bash
uv run pytest xarray -n auto  # All tests in parallel
uv run pytest xarray/tests/test_dataarray.py  # Specific file
```

## Linting & type checking

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files  # Includes ruff and other checks
uv run dmypy run  # Type checking with mypy
```

## Code Style Guidelines

### Import Organization

- **Always place imports at the top of the file** in the standard import section
- Never add imports inside functions or nested scopes unless there's a specific
  reason (e.g., circular import avoidance, optional dependencies in TYPE_CHECKING)
- Group imports following PEP 8 conventions:
  1. Standard library imports
  2. Related third-party imports
  3. Local application/library specific imports

## GitHub Interaction Guidelines

- **NEVER impersonate the user on GitHub**, always sign off with something like
  "[This is Claude Code on behalf of Jane Doe]"
- Never create issues nor pull requests on the xarray GitHub repository unless
  explicitly instructed
- Never post "update" messages, progress reports, or explanatory comments on
  GitHub issues/PRs unless specifically instructed
- When creating commits, always include a co-authorship trailer:
  `Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>`

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

I've implemented the missing tree-node operations. Everything in the task works in my own checks and in xarray's tree tests. The only test failures are 15 file-backend tests, which come from a broken HDF5 library in this environment rather than from these changes.

**What was missing**

- **`xarray/core/treenode.py`**: the file had blank gaps where most of the tree code had been removed. I filled them in:
  - the code that moves a node to a new parent or detaches it, including the checks that stop a node becoming its own parent or the child of one of its descendants;
  - the methods that look up or place an item by path;
  - all the "place in the tree" properties: `parents`, `root`, `siblings`, `level`, `depth`, `width`, `descendants`, `leaves`, `subtree` and `subtree_with_keys`;
  - the deprecated `ancestors` and `lineage` views, plus the older `iter_lineage`; all three warn every time they're used;
  - `group_subtrees` and `zip_subtrees`;
  - the step that gives a `NamedNode` the name it was stored under when it's attached.
- **Five other modules** use these functions but no longer imported them, so I added the imports back: `xarray/__init__.py` (which makes `xr.group_subtrees` public again), `core/datatree.py`, `core/formatting.py`, `core/datatree_mapping.py` and `backends/api.py`.

**Choices worth knowing about**

- **Error with no name happens first:** asking for a different parent without a child name used to detach the node from its old parent before raising the ValueError, leaving it orphaned. The check now runs before anything changes.
- **Immediate TypeError with no trees:** `group_subtrees()` and `zip_subtrees()` raise the TypeError as soon as they're called. A mismatch in tree structure is still raised only when iteration reaches that node.
- **Messages work for unnamed nodes:** the invalid-tree error messages show the node's repr rather than its name, because a plain `TreeNode` has no name.

**Testing**

- A script of my own covering each point in the task passes, and `ruff check` and `ruff format` are clean.
- Running the DataTree, mapping, formatting, concat, merge and DataTree-backend test files: 657 passed, 15 failed. Every failure involves h5netcdf; the h5netcdf tests I looked at all hit `RuntimeError: Unspecified error in H5DSis_scale` inside h5py. The netCDF4-only backend tests pass.
- Mypy finds no errors in `treenode.py`; its 2 reported errors are in `xarray/coding/cftimeindex.py`.
- I ran pytest and mypy with plain `python -m` because `uv` isn't installed here.

Nothing is committed.
